# @aponiajs/cron

> Declare scheduled jobs in an Aponia module, with the jobs read from a validated configuration. A thin adapter over `@elysia/cron` (which wraps croner): AponiaJS contributes a module a registration belongs in and a validated configuration the jobs come from, and no scheduling engine of its own.

**This is not a job queue.** There is no persistence, no retries, no cross-process coordination, and no distributed lock. A cron expression in one process runs in that process: two instances of an application running the same registration both run the same jobs, at the same moment, once each. A job that did not run because the process was down did not run, and nothing replays it. An application that needs work to happen exactly once across a fleet needs a different package.

**A reader who wants the raw plugin should use [`@elysia/cron`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@elysia/cron) directly.** Nothing here is unavailable there, and mounting it through an Aponia `PluginModule` costs a few lines. What this package adds is declaration through a module and validation of the options, and nothing else.

## What this package exports

```ts
import { CronModule, CronScheduler } from "@aponiajs/cron";
import type { CronJob, CronJobContext, CronJobOptions, CronConfiguration, CronModuleOptions } from "@aponiajs/cron";
```

- `CronModule` — `CronModule.register(options)` returns the `DynamicModule` an application's `imports` accepts.
- `CronScheduler` — the per-boot scheduler, which the module exports, so `application.get(CronScheduler)` reaches the boot's own jobs and the names the engine actually has.
- `CronJob`, `CronJobContext`, `CronJobOptions`, `CronConfiguration` — the job contract. `CronJobOptions` is derived from `@elysia/cron`'s own `CronConfig`, so it cannot drift from the engine.
- `CronModuleOptions` — `configuration`, `source`, and `key`.

## Declaring a scheduler

```ts
import { Module } from "@aponiajs/common";
import { CronModule } from "@aponiajs/cron";
import { CronConfig } from "./config.ts";

const scheduler = CronModule.register({ configuration: CronConfig });

@Module({ imports: [scheduler] })
export class AppModule {}
```

Both spellings mount the same module, and neither is lowered into the descriptor artifact `aponia build` writes. The build lowers an `imports` entry only when it is a single identifier naming a declaration read from the project's own source, and `CronModule.register({ ... })` returns a `DynamicModule` — a runtime value rather than such a declaration — so the module that names it is reported as `DECLINED` and left out of `descriptors.generated.ts` in every spelling, inline or held in a `const`. The scheduler still mounts and the application still boots; what is given up is the declared-graph boot.

`key` names the module's identity and defaults to `"cron"`. Two registrations that share one key are one module identity, which the graph refuses as a duplicate rather than quietly scheduling one set of jobs twice. One registration per application is the supported shape: two registrations with distinct keys both mount and both run, but they are one `CronScheduler` token, so reading one back raises `AMBIGUOUS_PROVIDER`. `source` overrides what the configuration's schema validates — a literal record instead of `process.env` — which is what a test passes.

## The validated configuration

The jobs come from a `defineConfiguration` declaration, not from an object literal. The schema validates the parameters; the transform that reads them builds the jobs, which is why a job's `run` can be a closure over the application's own services and its pattern can still be a value an operator set:

```ts
import { defineConfiguration } from "@aponiajs/common";
import { z } from "zod";

export const CronConfig = defineConfiguration(
  z
    .object({
      CRON_PATTERN: z.string().min(1).default("*/5 * * * * *"),
      CRON_TIMEZONE: z.string().min(1).default("UTC"),
    })
    .transform(({ CRON_PATTERN, CRON_TIMEZONE }) => ({
      jobs: [
        {
          name: "invoices",
          pattern: CRON_PATTERN,
          options: { timezone: CRON_TIMEZONE, protect: true },
          run: ({ options }) => sendInvoices({ protect: options.protect }),
        },
      ],
    })),
  "cron.config",
);
```

The module provides this token itself and exports it, so the application can read the same validated value back through `application.get(CronConfig)`.

## A job

`name` and `pattern` are both required and both must be non-empty; the scheduler checks that before it mounts anything. `pattern` is a cron expression, an ISO 8601 time, or a date, exactly as croner accepts it — six fields include seconds, five do not. `options` is forwarded to croner untouched: `timezone`, `maxRuns`, `protect`, `paused`, `startAt`, `stopAt`, `utcOffset`, `interval`, `legacyMode`, `context`, `catch`, `kill`, and `unref`. `run` is called once per tick with a frozen `CronJobContext` — the job's own `name`, `pattern`, and the options this package forwarded — and may be asynchronous. Its return value is ignored. `protect: true` skips a tick while the previous one is still running.

`run` receives a context, not the Elysia store. That is the one place this adapter's contract differs from the plugin it wraps: `@elysia/cron` calls `run` with the store — its own type claims `Cron`, which is not the value it passes — and a scheduled job here has no use for a store. A job lifted out of a raw `@elysia/cron` call needs its parameter changed and nothing else.

## Lifecycle

Jobs start when the module mounts — while the application is being built, before anything listens — and are ended by `application.close()`, whether or not the application ever listened. The stop runs through the boot's `CronScheduler.onApplicationShutdown`. One registration declared by one module class is one `DynamicModule`, so two applications built from it in one process hold two schedulers, and stopping one leaves the other's jobs running.

## Errors

A refused configuration raises `AponiaError` with `INVALID_CONFIGURATION_VALUE` — the schema rejected the value, or the value the schema produced is not a list of jobs — carrying `{ configuration, issues }` in both cases, so one shape covers a refusal wherever it landed. `INVALID_CONFIGURATION` is `provideConfiguration`'s own refusal of a declaration that is not a Standard Schema or whose validation answers asynchronously.

A job's own throw is not one of these. It is the engine's, it is not retried, and `options.catch` is how a job asks croner to survive one.
